newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish economic policy seen driven by elections.
newsitem.headline: Turkish economic policy seen driven by elections.

text.p: Turkey's new coalition government is expected to lean towards populist policies ahead of early elections rather than tackle the economy's deep-seated structural problems, economists said.
They forecast such a short-term approach will further fuel already rampant inflation, currently running at around an annual 75 percent.
And it will aggravate already weak public finances.

Both are areas which the International Monetary Fund has expressed concern about. An IMF mission to Turkey in April urged the government to enforce spending discipline and balance the budget as soon as possible.
"Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz is not strong enough to take radical measures to overcome the serious economic problems," Eser Karakas, a professor of economics at Istanbul University, told Reuters.

Conservative Yilmaz was appointed prime minister last week at the head of a secularist government, formed with the goal of ending months of political chaos. General elections are expected by mid-1998.
Election-driven policy is expected to include high public sector wage increases and further state aid for the large agriculture sector
"I think the government would prefer to establish an election-oriented economy. The average annual inflation base will soar by 10 to 12 percent next year after the general elections," Karakas added.
Karakas said there were alternatives to such policies that would address the country's basic economic problems.

"The alternative is to expand the taxpayer base and reduce public spending to bring down the public sector deficit, which stands at 10 percent of the country's gross national product, the highest of the OECD countries," he said.
"This is the only way to overcome the permanently high inflation," he added.
Turkey's taxpayer base represents only 16 percent of total voters, well below the 70 percent of industrialised countries.
Karakas said the government should add more rural workers and small-scale businesses to the taxpayer base.
"Unfortunately we cannot expect to apply such economic policies, but technically, the government has the chance to apply the alternative economic policies before the elections," he said.

Izzettin Onder, professor of economics at the same university, believed the new government had some leeway to introduce unpopular economic measures in view of the former Islamist-led government's deep rift with the broadbased secularist establishment.
"The government can take the necessary radical measures to solve the economy's deep problems with the society's strong support for its secularist struggle," Onder told Reuters.
"If the government can divert society's attention to the secularist struggle, it would not face any serious resistance from the people," he added.
Onder said the new government, which entered office this week, was taking over an economy in a ruinous state.
"Domestic debt (has) soared to more than 4,000 trillion lira ($26.7 billion) and it seems that the year-end budget deficit will increase to more than 2,000 trillion lira," he said.
It appeared the foreign trade deficit in 1997 would exceed the official target of $23.5 billion, and top $25 billion, he added. This compares with last year's $19.38 billion.
But Onder said he nevertheless thought the government would prefer to orient its policies to an early election.

"An election-oriented economy under a three-party coalition will cause deeper problems in the economy than a one party government, because each party will try to get a bigger share from the spending to get more votes," Onder said.

Karakas said the main political parties were all fearful of losing electoral support, given the even distribution of votes in the last election when the Islamist Welfare Party won with just over 20 percent of the vote.

"Because all their voting shares are close in percentage terms, if one of them loses 300,000 votes it could lose the election -- 500,000 additional votes would make Mesut Yilmaz the prime minister again," he added. ($ = 149960 Turkish Lire)
